title: Senior's toolkit: graphs in real code
summary: Build adjacency lists in one line, traverse without blowing the stack, run Dijkstra on PriorityQueue, and draw the graph when you are lost.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: graphs in real code
steps.body: Graphs show up at work as dependency trees, permissions, routes, org charts and grids. .NET has no graph type, so experienced developers build them from a few standard collections and know the traps: deep recursion and missing nodes.

toolkit.what: Build an adjacency list from a list of edges in one line. An `ILookup` returns an empty sequence for a node with no edges, so there is no `KeyNotFoundException`.
flags: when you must add edges later (a lookup is read-only)
for an undirected graph, add `(a, b)` and `(b, a)`
toolkit.example:
var deps = packages.SelectMany(p => p.DependsOn, (p, d) => (From: p.Name, To: d))
                   .ToLookup(e => e.From, e => e.To);

toolkit.what: Breadth-first search: fewest hops, levels, nearest match. Mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it, or it is queued many times.
flags: returns false if seen: check and mark in one call
record where you came from, to rebuild the path

toolkit.what: A recursive DFS on a big graph or grid can overflow the thread's stack (often 1 MB). A `StackOverflowException` cannot be caught: the process dies. An explicit stack lives on the heap.
flags: to visit them in the same order as the recursive version

toolkit.what: Shortest paths with weights. `PriorityQueue` has no decrease-key, so enqueue again when a distance improves and skip stale entries when they come out.
Grids are graphs whose neighbours you compute. A direction table plus one bounds check replaces four copies of the same `if`.
flags: visited set for a grid, cheaper than a HashSet
toolkit.example:
(int dr, int dc)[] dirs = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)];
foreach (var (dr, dc) in dirs) { int r = row + dr, c = col + dc; if ((uint)r < (uint)rows && (uint)c < (uint)cols) ... }

toolkit.what: Graphviz draws a graph from a text file of edges (`a -> b;`). When a dependency or workflow bug makes no sense, print the edges and look at the picture.
flags: draw left to right instead of top to bottom

steps.prompt: The flood-fill tool works on small images, then dies on a 2000 x 2000 one with this. A `try`/`catch` around the call does not help. What is the fix?
options: Rewrite `Fill` with an explicit `Stack<(int, int)>` (or a queue) instead of recursion
Run it in Release mode so the JIT removes the recursion
steps.explain: Each recursive call uses stack space, and one region can be millions of cells. .NET cannot catch a stack overflow; the process is terminated. An explicit stack grows on the heap, limited only by memory.

steps.prompt: Breadth-first search computes hops from node 1. What does this print?
steps.explain: `TryAdd` both checks and marks: node 4 is reached from 2 first, and the path through 3 is ignored. Because BFS goes level by level, the first time a node is reached is the fewest hops.

steps.prompt: Match each problem to the tool you reach for.
pairs: Fill a region of a huge grid
Build neighbours from a list of edges
See why the build order makes no sense

steps.prompt: A BFS over a social graph is correct but very slow, and memory grows far beyond the number of users. The code marks a node visited when it is **dequeued**. Why does that matter?
options: A node can be enqueued once by every neighbour before it is first dequeued. Mark it visited when you enqueue it
Marking on dequeue makes BFS return longer paths
steps.explain: In a dense graph the queue then holds a copy of a node per incoming edge: O(E) entries instead of O(V). The distances are still right, which is why this bug survives tests.

steps.prompt: Complete the Dijkstra loop that copes with `PriorityQueue` having no decrease-key.
code: while (pq.__1__(out var node, out var d))
if (d + w < dist[next]) { dist[next] = d + w; pq.__3__(next, d + w); }
steps.explain: Stale entries are those whose distance is larger than the best one already recorded. Equal is not stale: that is the entry that set `dist[node]`.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: For any traversal over data you do not control (user graphs, big grids, dependency trees), use an explicit stack or queue from the start. When graph code misbehaves, dump the edges to a `.dot` file and look at the drawing before debugging line by line.
